newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters talks continue, strike postponed.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters talks continue, strike postponed.

text.p: United Parcel Service and the Teamsters Union Friday continued their contract talks beyond a midnight deadline as they struggled to avert a strike that would cripple the nation's largest parcel carrier.
The Teamsters Union said in a statement that strike action against the company had been postponed until further notice and no time limit had been set on the talks.

UPS Chairman and Chief Executive Officer James Kelly and Teamsters President Ron Carey personally entered negotiations with the aid of a federal mediator around 7 p.m. EDT Thursday in a last-ditch bid to avert a strike.
"Talks are continuing at this time and they will continue as long as they make progress," Teamster spokesman Jeff Cappella said shortly after the midnight deadline elapsed without an agreement.
Another union spokesman, Rand Wilson, said it was premature to say strike action had been averted.

"We are ready (to strike). Our staff are in the local halls ready to go," adding that both sides agreed to continue the negotiations. "They will for as long as it's fruitful. There are a lot of people's lives on the line here."

Company spokeswoman Gina Ellrich said UPS workers would continue to deliver packages as the negotiations continued, with the help of a federal mediator, at the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service in downtown Washington DC.

"It is in everyone's best interest to reach an agreement, our customers and our employees, which is why we have always tried to move these contract talks along," Ellrich said. "We have every intention of continuing to operate."
A union spokeswoman said the decision to continue talks meant union members would not walk off their jobs after the deadline to agree a new contract elapsed.
Carey held out hope that an agreement could be reached just before talks between the two sides began.
"I am always optimistic and will continue to be so until 12 o'clock," Carey said, referring to a midnight deadline. "We're here to negotiate a contract, not a strike," he said.
Kelly, UPS CEO, declined comment before the talks began.
The negotiators were having to cope with increasingly uncomfortable conditions in the mediation service's ninth floor offices after the air conditioning went off, union sources said.

John Calhoun Wells, head of the federal mediation service -- which was founded by Congress to help avert major strikes -- said he asked the two parties to mount an eleventh-hour bid to reach agreement on a new contract.
He said they agreed to meet face to face, adding, "At this late stage, every step is like climbing a mountain."

But the company placed a full-page advertisement in Friday editions of the Washington Post -- which hit the streets well before the midnight deadline -- saying it was unable to reach an agreement with the Teamsters, but would do all it could to keep services operating.
"That tells me a little bit about the attitude of the company," Teamsters spokesman Wilson said when asked about the ad.
"They wrote the ad expecting a strike and in fact, they came back to the negotiating table," he said.
The two sides are negotiating a new five-year contract to replace the existing one, which expired at midnight.

If the talks fail and approximately 200,000 Teamsters decide to strike UPS, more than 12 million packages destined for roughly 1.5 million U.S. customers a day will be stranded, along with others overseas.
The key issues in the negotiations are creation of more full-time jobs, an end to subcontracting, safety, health and pension issues, the union said.
